section_summary: This section documents U.S. diplomatic and military monitoring of alleged Japanese propaganda, espionage, immigration, fishing, surveying, resource acquisition, and strategic reconnaissance in Mexico from 1934 to 1937. Reports focus especially on Baja California, Magdalena Bay, the Gulf of California, Sonora, and Mexico’s Pacific coast, but many allegations—particularly that Japan had landed arms or was building fortifications at Magdalena Bay—were subsequently discounted or attributed to Mexican naval construction. Later material concerns Japanese fishing expeditions, possible coastal and river surveys, proposed road and fishing concessions, petroleum interests, and U.S. interdepartmental efforts to assess Japanese population and immigration figures.

subfiles.title: Cover letter transmitting despatches on Japanese anti-American propaganda to the Navy Department
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Claude A. Swanson, Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Transmits confidential copies of Mexico City despatches concerning Japanese anti-American propaganda.
subfiles.summary: Welles forwards despatches dated July 7 and October 2, 1934, from the American Embassy in Mexico City. He notes that copies are also being sent to the War Department.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1582: Japanese Anti-American Propaganda
subfiles.from: R. Henry Norweb, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Reports on Japanese propaganda, reconnaissance, economic penetration, and immigration in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Norweb describes Japanese surveying parties, photography of Manzanillo, searches for strategic raw materials, propaganda, and rising legal and illegal immigration. He finds no clear evidence of direct anti-American propaganda but reports innuendo about a future U.S.–Japanese war. Although recommending vigilance, he judges Mexico’s ties to Japan to be weaker than its political, commercial, and cultural ties to the United States.

subfiles.title: Cover letter transmitting Japanese-propaganda despatches to the War Department
subfiles.from: Sumner Welles, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.to: George H. Dern, Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Forwards confidential embassy reporting about Japanese anti-American propaganda in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: This is the War Department counterpart of the preceding Navy transmittal. It encloses the July 7 despatch and states that copies are also being forwarded to the Navy Department.

subfiles.title: Duplicate copy of Despatch No. 1583: Japanese Anti-American Propaganda
subfiles.from: R. Henry Norweb, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Duplicates the embassy assessment of Japanese political, commercial, and intelligence-related activity in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The despatch recounts Japanese coastal surveying, resource prospecting, propaganda, and immigration into Baja California and the Pacific coast. It distinguishes insinuating pro-Japanese messaging from demonstrable direct anti-American propaganda. Norweb concludes that reputed Mexican–Japanese rapprochement is more apparent than real but merits close observation.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on delaying distribution of Despatch No. 1582
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Recommends awaiting further reporting before sending the July despatch to the War and Navy Departments.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs advises that the Department first await Mexico City’s directed investigation of Japanese consular officers. Only after that report arrives should it decide whether to furnish Despatch No. 1582 to military departments.

subfiles.title: Interdivisional routing and marginal-action sheets
subfiles.from: Department of State, Divisions of Mexican and Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Records largely illegible internal routing concerning the Japanese-propaganda reports.
subfiles.summary: These pages consist chiefly of division headings, marginal notations, and fragmentary instructions. The legible portions appear connected with the decision whether the material should go to the War and Navy Departments.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 1821: Japanese Anti-American Propaganda
subfiles.from: Josephus Daniels, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Reports the result of an investigation into alleged Japanese entertainment of Mexican officials and anti-American propaganda.
subfiles.summary: The embassy consulted the consuls at Mexicali, Ensenada, Guaymas, and Mazatlán. It found no evidence corroborating the rumored Japanese activity and had nothing to add to the July despatch.

subfiles.title: Navy Department acknowledgment of State Department propaganda reports
subfiles.from: Navy Department
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the July and October embassy despatches on Japanese propaganda.
subfiles.summary: The Navy Department confirms receipt of the State Department’s October 13 transmittal and its enclosures. It expresses appreciation for being kept informed.

subfiles.title: War Department acknowledgment of embassy despatches
subfiles.from: Chief of Staff, War Department
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of Despatches Nos. 1582 and 1821 concerning Japanese propaganda.
subfiles.summary: The Chief of Staff writes at the Secretary of War’s request. The letter thanks the State Department for information concerning Japanese anti-American propaganda in Mexico.

subfiles.title: Second Navy Department acknowledgment
subfiles.from: Navy Department
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the State Department’s October 13 letter and enclosures.
subfiles.summary: This brief communication records receipt of file ME 894.20212/358. Its enclosures are not discussed substantively.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to report on Baja California Sur
subfiles.from: American Consulate, Guaymas; indexed under Ray
subfiles.about: Points to a report on political, religious, and Japanese conditions in the southern territory of Baja California.
subfiles.summary: The sheet directs researchers to file 812.00-Lower California/184. The referenced report arose from a recent trip through the territory and covered Japanese as well as political and religious conditions.

subfiles.title: War Department Intelligence Division distribution and forwarding sheets
subfiles.from: War Department Intelligence Division
subfiles.to: War Department and State Department offices
subfiles.about: Provides distribution options and a handwritten forwarding notation for intelligence material.
subfiles.summary: The printed form lists War Department branches and State Department regional divisions. The following page contains a mostly illegible handwritten note apparently accompanying the routed material.

subfiles.title: Confidential letter alleging Japanese espionage on Mexico’s Pacific coast
subfiles.from: Elias García Cuadra
subfiles.about: A Mexican traveling salesman alleges that Japanese commercial, fishing, and propaganda activities conceal military espionage.
subfiles.summary: García Cuadra describes Japanese residents, failing businesses allegedly subsidized by Japan, a propagandist’s lectures, fishing vessels making coastal surveys, and a report of secretly landed aircraft parts. He argues that Mexico’s security is tied to that of the United States and urges counter-propaganda and preventive action. He offers to provide further confidential information through an address in Mazatlán.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs note recommending disclosure to the Navy
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Recommends giving the Navy all available information about suspicious material near a proposed Mexican naval base.
subfiles.summary: The note observes that the latest Guaymas despatch identifies the material as probably belonging to the Mexican Government. It recommends letting the Navy decide whether any further investigation is warranted.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs memorandum on proposed Magdalena Bay investigation
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Questions whether Despatch No. 87 justifies the expense of an on-site consular investigation.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs agrees that the evidence does not warrant the proposed travel expense. It asks whether Military or Naval Intelligence has funds or facilities and suggests sharing pertinent excerpts in strict confidence.

subfiles.title: Handwritten Far Eastern Affairs consultation note
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Records an internal consultation, apparently involving Stanley K. Hornbeck and Captain William D. Puleston.
subfiles.summary: The handwriting is mostly illegible. The readable names and fragments indicate discussion with Naval Operations about how the matter should be handled.

subfiles.title: Mexican Affairs memorandum opposing consular travel to Magdalena Bay
subfiles.from: Division of Mexican Affairs
subfiles.about: Finds that the available evidence does not justify sending a Guaymas consular officer to Magdalena Bay.
subfiles.summary: The writer considers the expense and absence from duty unwarranted on the information presented. The note remains open to reconsideration and asks whether confidential extracts should instead be sent to Military and Naval Intelligence.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 87: Japanese Activities in the Gulf of California and on the West Coast of Mexico
subfiles.from: Guy W. Ray, American Vice Consul, Guaymas
subfiles.about: Reports rumors of Japanese arms and fortifications, shipping and fishing ventures, scrap purchases, and agricultural activity.
subfiles.summary: Ray discusses reports of cement, cannon, and ammunition in Magdalena Bay, while recognizing that the material might belong to a Mexican naval-base project or a revolutionary plot. He details Japanese-crewed fishing vessels, the expected Banshu Maru, ship dismantling and scrap exports, Tadahiro Tamaki’s travels, and interest in cotton cultivation. Although skeptical of the fortification story, he recommends vigilance and suggests that Mexico restrict Japanese fishing and other concessions.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 97: Japanese Activities
subfiles.from: Guy W. Ray, American Vice Consul, Guaymas
subfiles.about: Retracts the implication that a foreign power landed military supplies at Magdalena Bay.
subfiles.summary: Ray quotes a reliable American resident who confirmed with Governor Juan Domínguez that Mexico was building a naval base at Magdalena Bay. He concludes that the cement and other materials were almost certainly placed there by the Mexican Government, though the earlier rumors had seemed sufficiently consistent to report.

subfiles.title: State Department transmittal of Guaymas despatches to the Navy
subfiles.from: Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Forwards three Guaymas despatches concerning Japanese activities and Magdalena Bay.
subfiles.summary: The note follows a conversation between the Far Eastern Affairs chief and Captain William D. Puleston. It highlights the latest evidence that cement and other supplies at Magdalena Bay were intended for a Mexican naval base serving ships purchased in Spain.

subfiles.title: Far Eastern Affairs abstract of Japanese-activities reporting
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Guaymas report, newspaper article, naval inquiry, and proposed Japanese shrimp shipment.
subfiles.summary: The abstract describes a Mexican newspaper’s warning that Mexico could become another Belgium in a U.S.–Japanese war. It also records a Mexican naval officer’s rejection of the Magdalena Bay munitions story and Mexican approval for a Japanese vessel to load shrimp at Guaymas.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 108: Japanese Activities
subfiles.from: Guy W. Ray, American Vice Consul, Guaymas
subfiles.about: Transmits and comments on a Mexican newspaper article alleging Japanese strategic activity along the Pacific coast.
subfiles.summary: Ray regards the article’s open criticism of Japan as more unusual than its largely familiar allegations. He reports continuing suspicion of a Japanese traveling salesman, official rejection of the Magdalena Bay rumor, planned Japanese shrimp purchases, and Japanese communities in the Yaqui Valley, Ciudad Obregón, and Navojoa. He concludes that local sentiment would favor the United States over Japan and that Japanese interest in the region probably exceeds purely commercial motives.

subfiles.title: “Baja California, Área de Combate”
subfiles.from: Heraldo del Yaqui
subfiles.about: Claims that Japan maintains an intelligence system and is preparing Baja California for possible operations against the United States.
subfiles.summary: The article invokes Floyd Gibbons and Fred Pasley while alleging Japanese espionage among fishermen, merchants, restaurateurs, and farmers. It discusses a possible air base near Ensenada, the strategic position of Mexicali and Todos Santos Bay, and the risk that Mexico could be invaded like Belgium. It nevertheless argues that Mexico’s present government is friendlier to the United States and unlikely to assist Japanese plans.

subfiles.title: Translation of “Baja California, Area of Combat”
subfiles.from: Heraldo del Yaqui; translated for the American Consulate
subfiles.about: Provides an English translation of the Spanish article alleging Japanese preparations in Baja California.
subfiles.summary: The translation repeats allegations of a Japanese intelligence network, an Ensenada landing field, extensive Japanese fishing, and strategic use of Todos Santos Bay. It presents Mexico as a potential victim like Belgium in a conflict between Japan and the United States. The article also emphasizes the logistical hazards Japan would face in fighting far from its homeland.

subfiles.title: Military Intelligence Division routing form
subfiles.from: Military Intelligence Division, G-2
subfiles.about: Provides internal distribution and action options for attached intelligence correspondence.
subfiles.summary: The form lists administrative, intelligence, operations, geographic, and public-relations branches. It contains no substantive intelligence beyond its routing function.

subfiles.title: Naval Intelligence letter transmitting report on Japanese travelers to Mexico
subfiles.from: John Stapler, Acting Director of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.to: J. F. McGurk, Assistant Chief of Latin American Affairs
subfiles.about: Transmits an Eleventh Naval District report about Japanese officials traveling by air to Mexico.
subfiles.summary: Stapler forwards a copy of the naval-district commandant’s letter. The State Department routed it as information relevant to Mexican affairs.

subfiles.title: Eleventh Naval District report: Japanese en route to Mexico
subfiles.from: W. T. Tarrant, Commandant, Eleventh Naval District
subfiles.to: Chief of Naval Operations, Director of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: Reports unusually heavy Japanese air travel from California to Mexico City.
subfiles.summary: Lieutenant Commander Donald Armstrong reported that six to ten Japanese per day had recently flown from San Francisco and Los Angeles to Mexico City. Their passports showed origins in Tokyo and suggested official status, and Mexican consular officials reportedly gave them every consideration.

subfiles.title: Reply thanking Naval Intelligence for the Japanese-travel report
subfiles.from: Edwin C. Wilson
subfiles.to: John Stapler, Acting Director of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the naval report and forwards it to the chief of the Mexican Division.
subfiles.summary: Wilson thanks Stapler for the letter concerning Japanese travelers bound for Mexico. He states that he has sent it to Edward Reed because of its relevance to Mexican affairs.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on a reported Japanese highway contract and Clipperton Island
subfiles.from: Unidentified State Department officer
subfiles.about: Records claims relayed by Mr. Morgan about Japanese road construction in Mexico and French fortification of Clipperton Island.
subfiles.summary: Morgan reported that a Japanese firm allegedly contracted to build a highway from Mexico City to Guadalajara and possibly onward to Mazatlán, suggesting political as well as economic significance. He also relayed Mexican resentment over France’s acquisition of Clipperton Island and rumors that France was fortifying it. The writer doubted the highway report and directed Morgan to discuss both matters with the Mexican Division.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference and opening fragment of comprehensive report on Japanese activities
subfiles.from: Leavitt, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Points to and introduces a comprehensive report on Japanese governmental and commercial activity in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The cross-reference directs researchers to file 812.154/268. The surviving introductory paragraph says that Japanese government-linked companies appeared very active in Mexico, but the writer could not determine what ultimate results they sought.

subfiles.title: First Cavalry Division report on Dr. Pablo R. Nikami
subfiles.from: A. T. Lackey, G-2, First Cavalry Division
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Eighth Corps Area
subfiles.about: Reports suspicious travel, photography, and technical interests of a Japanese national in northern Mexico.
subfiles.summary: A reliable El Paso informant stated that Dr. Pablo R. Nikami traveled with extensive pack equipment between Temósachic and El Valle while ostensibly prospecting. Nikami reportedly photographed dams and irrigation works at Las Delicias, possessed ample funds, and displayed expertise in geology, metallurgy, chemistry, and medicine.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 162 on Japanese fishing
subfiles.from: A. F. Yepis, Guaymas
subfiles.about: Points to correspondence about Japanese fishing and other activity in the Gulf of California.
subfiles.summary: The referenced despatch reproduced two letters sent by Fred Lewellyn to the local manager of Pan American Fisheries. The index notes that parts of the situation described in the letters appeared to contain some truth.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Despatch No. 164 on Japanese fishing
subfiles.from: A. F. Yepis, Guaymas
subfiles.about: Points to Pan American Fisheries correspondence concerning Japanese activity in the Gulf of California.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references file 812.628/284 and Despatch No. 164. Its subject is Japanese fishing activity and related commercial correspondence.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 164: Possible Fishing and Other Activities of Japanese in the Gulf of California
subfiles.from: A. F. Yepis, American Vice Consul, Guaymas
subfiles.about: Transmits another Fred Lewellyn letter about possible Japanese plans in the Gulf of California.
subfiles.summary: Yepis encloses Lewellyn’s October 15 letter at the request of the Pan American Fisheries manager. He cautions that the consulate cannot vouch for its accuracy, although some assertions may be true and of interest.

subfiles.title: Fred Lewellyn letter on Japanese commercial and political intentions
subfiles.from: Fred Lewellyn
subfiles.about: Relays conversations alleging Japanese plans to obtain Gulf concessions and gain control of Mexican enterprises.
subfiles.summary: Lewellyn describes contacts with Japanese visitors named Date and Onishi, who questioned him closely about Mexico and the Gulf of California. He alleges that a Japanese group paid a prominent Mexican official for help securing a concession and sought concealed participation in established concerns. He warns that Japan intended to become heavily involved in Mexico and urges resistance to its efforts.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Ensenada despatch on road, fishing, and reconnaissance plans
subfiles.from: American Consulate, Ensenada; indexed under Samel
subfiles.about: Points to a report linking a proposed Japanese road-and-fishing agreement to coastal reconnaissance.
subfiles.summary: The sheet summarizes allegations that the Minato Maru’s exploratory work concealed military and naval reconnaissance. It also notes Tamanosuke Suzuki’s efforts to obtain information about Guadalupe Island.

subfiles.title: Despatch on Japanese activities on the west coast of Mexico
subfiles.from: American Consul at Ensenada, indexed as Samel
subfiles.about: Reports suspicions that the Minato Maru expedition and Japanese residents were gathering strategic geographic information.
subfiles.summary: A Mexican shipmaster and naval reserve officer alleged that the Minato Maru’s exploration masked military and naval reconnaissance and identified Japanese personnel and a Mexican interpreter attached to the mission. Reports from Yavaros claimed ostensibly linguistic classes centered on maps and charts. Tamanosuke Suzuki also questioned the informant about Guadalupe Island’s topography and possible use as an aircraft landing field.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Standard-Vacuum letter on Japanese oil interests
subfiles.from: P. W. Parker, Standard-Vacuum Oil Company, New York City
subfiles.about: Points to information on Japanese individuals seeking oil concessions in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The underlying letter concerned movements of Japanese believed interested in acquiring Mexican petroleum concessions. The substantive letter is filed elsewhere under 812.6363/2891.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Embassy Despatch No. 3464
subfiles.from: Josephus Daniels, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Points to the Japanese minister’s remarks on Japanese fishing and petroleum activities in Mexico.
subfiles.summary: The indexed despatch records comments by the Japanese minister. Its principal subjects were Japanese fishing and oil activity in Mexico.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Embassy Despatch No. 3549
subfiles.from: Josephus Daniels, American Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Points to a confidential list of petroleum concessions obtained by a Japanese-controlled Mexican company.
subfiles.summary: The underlying memorandum concerned the Compañía Mexicana de Petróleo. It listed concessions reportedly obtained by the Japanese-controlled company to that date.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Arizona governor’s correspondence on Japanese fishing
subfiles.from: Governor of Arizona
subfiles.about: Points to letters from A. L. Verdugo and Bert Caudry about Japanese fishing in the Gulf of California.
subfiles.summary: The sheet references file 812.628/342. The underlying correspondence concerned Japanese fishing activities and included letters from Verdugo and Caudry.

subfiles.title: Fort Huachuca letter reporting Japanese coastal and inland surveys
subfiles.from: John F. Franklin, Commanding Officer, Fort Huachuca
subfiles.to: F. D. Mallon, G-2, Eighth Corps Area
subfiles.about: Relays reports of Japanese charting, coastal colonies, a scientific vessel, and survey activity in Sonora.
subfiles.summary: An informant alleged that a Japanese steamer and sampans were charting the Gulf of California while colonies of men served as survey stations. Another party of five Japanese and a Mexican engineer was reportedly surveying the Yaqui River while posing as prospectors. The letter also reports a Mexican seizure of machine guns and pistols at Empalme and summarizes an agrarian dispute in the Yaqui Valley.

subfiles.title: Eighth Corps Area report on Japanese petroleum activity
subfiles.from: F. D. Mallon, Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, Eighth Corps Area
subfiles.to: Assistant Chief of Staff, G-2, War Department
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese acquisition and prospective development of Mexican oil concessions.
subfiles.summary: Walter B. Pyron stated that Japanese governmental representatives had long sought oil in the Isthmus region and had obtained concessions there and in Tamaulipas and Nuevo León. He believed development might begin in southern Veracruz, with oil moved by rail to Salina Cruz for export. The report also briefly notes increasingly difficult labor demands on the Gulf Refining Company.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on reported Japanese activities in Baja California
subfiles.from: Edward L. Reed, Division of Mexican Affairs
subfiles.about: Reviews departmental evidence concerning Japanese activity, population, and immigration privileges in Baja California.
subfiles.summary: Reed finds no reports of intensified Japanese activity beyond apparently legitimate fishing ventures and a few unconfirmed rumors. He also finds no evidence of an abnormally large recent influx of Japanese into Baja California. He explains that treaty-based Japanese immigration privileges had been terminated by a 1924 agreement between Mexico and Japan.

subfiles.title: War Department request for Japanese population and immigration data
subfiles.doc_type: letter with State Department routing note
subfiles.from: E. M. Hammond, Chief, Latin American Section, G-2
subfiles.to: Chief, Division of Mexican Affairs, Department of State
subfiles.about: Requests statistics and reporting on Japanese residents, immigration, and coastal surveys in Mexico and Baja California.
subfiles.summary: The War Department asks for the number of Japanese in Mexico and Lower California, recent immigration totals, and the frequency of coastal-area surveys or reports. Page 310 contains a largely illegible Mexican Affairs notation concerning preparation or routing of the requested information.
